comments.author: Alexander Terp
comments.body:
**Plan for the slot-3 round, posted before building. Measured first: the 1024 is not
one bug, and it is not herdr's.**

## What the measurements say

Everything below was recorded against the pinned herdr 0.8.0 and, where it says so, against
a bare pty with no daemon in it at all.

**1. `pane send` and the keyboard use different daemon verbs, and only one of them is
mode-aware.** `muster pane send` builds `pane.send_text`, which observations section 5 already
records as a raw write to the pane's PTY - herdr does not parse those bytes. Muster's own paste,
from the keyboard, goes through `pane.send_input`, which the daemon encodes against the pane's
live `input_state()`. Into a raw-mode program that had enabled DEC 2004:

    pane.send_text   "line one\nline two\nline three"  ->  line one\nline two\nline three
    pane.send_input  "line one\nline two\nline three"  ->  ESC[200~line one\nline two\nline threeESC[201~

So every newline in a `pane send` payload reaches a harness as a bare newline, which a harness
reading a bracketed paste takes as a submission. A multi-line brief becomes several submissions
and the last line is the prompt. That is the second failure this card describes - "an
instruction arrived as its last four words" - and it is Muster's bug, not herdr's.

**2. The 1024 is the receiving pane's tty, not herdr and not Muster.** `pane.send_text` carried
10,000 bytes intact into a raw-mode reader; so did `pane.send_input`. The cap appears only when
the program in the pane has left the terminal in canonical mode - `cat`, a script reading stdin,
anything with no line editor. Measured on a bare pty, no daemon involved:

    canonical mode, draining reader
      1023 bytes + LF  ->  reader saw 1024
      1024 bytes + LF  ->  reader saw 0

That is `MAX_CANON`. And the failure is worse than truncation: the whole line is discarded, not
cut. What made it read as "exactly 1024" is the echo - the tty puts the first 1024 characters on
the screen and then drops the line when the terminator arrives. Reproduced end to end through
the pinned daemon into a pane running `cat`: 1024 bytes written to the file, 1030 bytes wrote
nothing at all.

A shell prompt is not this case. zle and readline run in raw mode, so an interactive shell has no
1024 limit either.

## What I am building

**Route `SendText` through `pane.send_input`.** The verb the keyboard already uses, so the CLI and
the chord stop encoding the same act two different ways. herdr decides whether to fence, from the
pane's real state, which is the whole reason that verb exists. Fixes the newline failure; leaves the
canonical-mode case where it belongs, which is in the receiving tty. Conformance cases and their
`why` move with it.

**`muster pane send --confirm`.** A field on `SendToPane`, handled in the core, not in the CLI - the
CLI stays a pure client. After the send and the Return it reads the pane back and refuses if what
was sent is not visible there. Whitespace-insensitive, against a bounded tail of the payload, so a
wrap does not read as a miss.

What it honestly proves is arrival, not submission: reading the screen cannot tell a submitted
prompt from one sitting in the input, because both draw the text. `a_2I7Acusq4` asks for "still
sitting in the input unsubmitted" and I am not building that - I can find no way to tell the two
apart from a pane's text that is not a guess about one harness's layout. What `--confirm` does
catch is the case this card is about: a line the tty dropped, which is nowhere on the pane.

**Say both in `muster docs limits`**, and stop `--enter`'s help text promising submission.

**Record the verbs.** A `send-text` scenario in `tools/herdr-probe/`, a transcript under
`corpus/herdr-0.8.0/send-text/`, and a section in `docs/observations/herdr-0.8.0.md` - so a herdr
re-pin re-records whether `send_input` still fences, which is the fact this now rests on. The
bare-pty measurement goes in beside it as the control that shows the cap is not herdr's.

## a_2I8fSrotB, doctor - cause found, and it is a fourth one

Not any of the three the card asks between. **`pgrep` excludes its own ancestors by default**
(`man pgrep`, `-a`). `./dev --doctor` run from inside a Muster pane has the app's daemon as an
ancestor - launchd, then `herdr server`, then the pane's shell, then rad, then pgrep - so the one
daemon holding live agents is the one process pgrep structurally will not report. Measured here:

    pgrep -x herdr      ->  16682 16919 56602 63224 63390 63567
    pgrep -a -x herdr   ->  16682 16919 20747 56602 63224 63390 63567

20747 is `/Applications/Muster.app/Contents/Library/MusterSessions.app/Contents/MacOS/herdr
server`, and walking my own ppid chain reaches it in four hops. Socket discovery was never the
problem: `lsof -a -p 20747 -U` names `~/.config/herdr/sessions/muster/herdr.sock` correctly.

This also explains the 2026-09-02 run reading as nine clients and no daemon. Most of what pgrep
does find is `herdr terminal session control <pane>` - a pane's bridge, correctly reported as
having no API socket, and useless as a row. Naming those for what they are is the second half.

Validation bullet 2 - a daemon whose binary was replaced is still listed - holds by construction,
since pgrep matches `p_comm`, which is set at exec and outlives the file. It gets a test rather
than an argument.

## a_2I7ASgulK, the contract tier - the open question, decided

The card leaves it open whether `main()` should stop what the last run left, or each check should
own its daemon's life. **Both, and they are not the same mechanism.**

Each check owns its daemon, through one shared helper spelled
`HERDR_SOCKET_PATH=<socket> <pinned herdr> server stop`. That is faults 1 and 2, and it removes
both spellings that silently did nothing - the popped `HERDR_SESSION` and the `--socket` option
herdr 0.8.0 does not have.

And `main()` stops what a previous run left before deleting `ROOT`, because a run that is
interrupted never reaches its `finally`, and deleting the socket first is what makes a stray
unreachable by anything but a signal. Recovery for the case the first mechanism cannot cover,
rather than a second way of doing the same job.

Third: the tier asserts it. After the checks, nothing under `ROOT` may still be answering, and a
run that leaked says so and fails. The card's first validation bullet is a thing somebody has to
re-measure with `./dev --doctor`; this makes the tier prove it itself.

## Order

Verbs and the observation first, since everything else in this card rests on the measurement.
Then `--confirm` and the docs, then doctor, then the contract tier - which I can verify, since
this machine has the GUI session and the daemon `--contract` needs.

comments.author: Alexander Terp
comments.body:
**Done, and the card describes two failures with two different causes. Neither is a 1024-byte cap in Muster or in herdr.**

**The multi-line half was Muster's, and is fixed.** `muster pane send` built `pane.send_text`, a raw write to the pane's PTY. Muster's own paste, from the keyboard, has always used `pane.send_input`, which the daemon encodes against the pane's live modes. Only the second is fenced as a bracketed paste. Measured against the pinned daemon, into a raw-mode program that had enabled DEC 2004:

    pane.send_text   "line one\nline two\nline three"  ->  line one\nline two\nline three
    pane.send_input  "line one\nline two\nline three"  ->  ESC[200~line one\nline two\nline threeESC[201~

So every newline in a CLI send arrived at a harness as a submission, and the harness read the last line as the whole prompt. That is "an instruction arrived as its last four words". Both `pane send` and `pane new --run` now go out on `pane.send_input`.

**The 1024 is the receiving terminal's, and nothing above it can raise it.** Both verbs carried ten thousand bytes intact into a program that had taken the terminal for itself, which every agent harness has. The cap appears only when the program in the pane left the terminal in canonical mode - `cat`, a script reading stdin, anything without a line editor. An interactive shell is not this case, because zle and readline run raw.

| A line of | A canonical-mode pane read | A bare pty read |
|---|---|---|
| 1001 bytes | 1001 | 1001 |
| 1024 bytes | 1024 | 1024 |
| 1025 bytes | 0 | 0 |
| 2201 bytes | 0 | 0 |

Terminator included on both sides. The right column is a pty the probe forks with no daemon anywhere near it, answering identically - so this is `MAX_CANON` in the line discipline.

**And it is discard, not truncation**, which is what made it read as a clean cut. The tty echoes the first thousand-odd characters to the screen and then drops the whole line when the terminator arrives. The measurement in this card's description read the echo and concluded 1024 bytes had landed. None of it had.

Recorded as section 25 of `docs/observations/herdr-0.8.0.md`, with a `sending-text` probe scenario and the transcript under `corpus/herdr-0.8.0/sending-text/` - so a herdr re-pin re-records whether `send_input` still fences, which is the fact `pane send` now rests on.

**The silence is answered by `pane send --confirm`** (a_2I7Acusq4), which reads the pane back and exits non-zero if what was sent is not on it. A discarded line is a refusal now rather than an exit 0.

**Both workarounds this card recorded can go.** A multi-line message is one send. Sending text and Return separately is no longer needed for correctness - what `--enter` cannot promise is that the harness submits, which is documented rather than worked around.

creator: Alexander Terp
description:
`muster pane send` delivers at most 1024 bytes and drops the rest with no error. The command exits 0, so the sender believes the whole message landed and the receiving agent acts on a fragment.

Measured 2026-09-01 while driving three worker agents in a 2x2 grid. A pane running `cat` was sent a 2200-byte single-line payload of position-marked tokens; the pane received exactly 1024. Repeated with a 1496-byte payload: cut at the identical byte. The boundary is exact, not approximate.

What makes this expensive rather than annoying is that the failure is silent on both ends. An agent receiving a truncated instruction has no way to know it was truncated - it reads a coherent-looking fragment and acts on it. In the session that found this, an instruction to a worker arrived as its last four words, "ll reconsider. Otherwise carry on.", the tail of "...say so and I will reconsider." The worker reasonably replied asking what it should reconsider. Three separate messages in that session were cut mid-word, in both directions.

A second failure mode compounds it, and may be the same bug or a different one: newlines in the payload appear to submit early, so a multi-line message to a TUI becomes several submissions and only the last is seen as the prompt. Worth checking whether that is the 1024 cap interacting with line-buffered input or something separate.

Two workarounds found, worth documenting even if the cap is lifted. Send text and Return separately - `pane send` with the text, pause, then a second `pane send` with an empty string and `--enter` - because `--enter` on a long paste races and the Return can arrive mid-paste. And for anything genuinely long, write it to a file and send a one-line `read <path>`; three briefs of 140-160 lines delivered that way arrived intact first time.

Whatever the fix, the silence is the part that matters: refusing oversized input with an error would be better than delivering half of it.
title: pane send silently truncates at 1024 bytes
